Korea and Vietnam, 1950–1973

Eleven battles from Task Force Smith at Osan in 1950 to Hamburger Hill in 1969: the first American fight in Korea, the Marines at Fox Hill, the perimeter at Chipyong-ni, the Commonwealth brigade at Kapyong, the hills of Heartbreak Ridge and Pork Chop, the landing zone at X-Ray, Hill 875 at Dak To, Hill 861A at Khe Sanh, the street fighting in Hue and the A Shau valley. Every rule is in the Rules; this book holds the armies' figures for both wars, the wound tables their battles roll on, the battlefields, and a rifle squad in Vietnam followed through one night.

The battlefields: Task Force Smith at Osan 1950, Fox Hill at Toktong Pass 1950, The perimeter at Chipyong-ni 1951, Hill 504 and the valley at Kapyong 1951, Hill 931 on Heartbreak Ridge 1951, Pork Chop Hill 1953, Landing zone X-Ray 1965, Hill 875 1967, Hill 861A 1968, Hue: the new city 1968, Hamburger Hill 1969.

What is switched on

All four modules but the first: Modern fire, Armour and mines, and Air and night devices, with helicopters and landing by air from Vietnam on, and night vision (infrared searchlights) in Vietnam. The wounded go out by helicopter where a landing zone and a helicopter are left, as the Rules' After the battle says; else by motor ambulance. Wounds heal and fester as the Rules' Recovery says: it does not yet count the antibiotics of these wars.

Trouble at work

Korean War (1950-1953)

d10 Trouble
1 MPs search his kit and find goods or money he can't explain.
2 A surprise MPC conversion day: whatever old MPC he holds is worthless.
3 Shelling or a night raid hits the work site.
4 He walks into an unmarked friendly minefield.
5 The pay never comes: the boss pocketed the payroll.
6 A refugee family begs him to get them south.
7 Accused of working for the North: counter-intelligence asks questions.
8 Typhus or frostbite: a week lost.
9 R&R goes bad: robbed, or brawling with the shore patrol.
10 A Korean co-worker vanishes, and his family thinks he knows where.

Vietnam War (1965-1973)

d10 Trouble
1 A CID inquiry into currency or PX goods.
2 A surprise MPC conversion day: locals holding old MPC beg him to swap it.
3 A rocket or sapper attack on the site.
4 The VC tax collector demands a share, or else.
5 A road mine or booby trap on the way to work.
6 His pay is skimmed by a camp commander or a boss.
7 Heroin or a bad bar fight costs a week and his name.
8 Inflation: wages buy a fifth less this month.
9 The aircraft is shot up: walk out through hostile ground.
10 A co-worker is VC, and he knows that he knows.

What each skill is for

Korean War (1950-1953)

Skill Use Usually Against Success Failure Fumble
Persuade Haggle: Beat down a price. Ordinary the seller (Persuade) A tenth off (a quarter on a critical). The list price. No sale today.
Persuade Find a billet: Talk a village or a householder into a bed and a meal. Ordinary the householder or headman (Presence) Fed and bedded tonight: no keep to pay. He pays his keep, or sleeps rough. The village turns against the party: trouble.
Persuade Talk past a guard: Get by a sentry, a gate or the provost without the right papers. Hard the sentry or provost (Wits) Through. Turned back. Held as a deserter or a spy.
Persuade Question a prisoner: Get a prisoner or a local to talk. Ordinary the prisoner (Nerve) He tells what he knows (the GM decides how much is true). Nothing. He lies, and is believed.
Command Drive a hard task: Get men to do something hard and tiring: dig all night, march on after dark, cross a river. Ordinary — Done. Done slowly, or only half. They refuse.
Command Keep order: Stop plunder, drinking or a mutinous mood. Hard — They obey. Some slip away to it. They turn on him.
Letters Read or write: Read an order, a letter or a map's names; write a report. Easy — Read or written. Slowly, or with mistakes. He gets it wrong and does not know it.
Letters Forge a pass: Make a pass, an order or a billeting ticket that will be believed. Hard whoever checks it (Watch) It passes. Doubted: Talk past a guard instead. Seen through: held as a deserter or a spy.
Craft Mend kit: Mend a weapon, harness, boots, a cart or a radio set; a day's work. Ordinary — Mended. Not yet: another day. Ruined.
Craft Make something: Make ladders, a raft, a shelter, snowshoes or a litter from what is to hand. Ordinary — Made. Takes twice as long. It fails when it is used.
Drive Drive under pressure: Drive off the road, at night without lights, or under fire. Ordinary — Through. Slowed or lost. Ditched or overturned.
Fieldcraft Track: Follow men or animals. Ordinary the men being followed (Stealth) On their trail. Lost it. On the wrong trail.
Fieldcraft Find the way: Cross country without roads or a guide; at night, hard. Ordinary — On the way. Half a day lost. Lost: a day, or into the enemy.
Fieldcraft Hunt or gather: Find food or water for himself in the country. Ordinary — Fed today: no keep to pay. Nothing found. Something that makes him ill.
Watch Spot: See an ambush, a man hiding, a trap or a thing out of place. Ordinary whoever is hiding (Stealth) Seen. Missed. Sure there is nothing there.
Watch Search: Search a house, a body or a baggage wagon. Easy — Found what there is. Missed it. Missed it and left traces.
Stealth Sneak: Get past sentries, into a camp or away from one. Ordinary the sentries (Watch) Unseen. Seen, but not yet caught. Walks into them.
Stealth Steal: Lift a purse, a horse or rations unseen. Hard the owner or the guard (Watch) Taken. Not taken. Caught in the act: the provost.
Leechcraft Diagnose: Tell what a sick man has, and whether it will spread. Ordinary — Named: the GM tells which sickness. Unsure. Wrong.
Signals Get through: Raise another station, mend a line or a set, or send a message in code. Ordinary — Through. Not yet: try again next hour. The set or line is out until mended.
Strength Force or carry: Force a door, lift a beam, carry a wounded man. Ordinary — Done. Not alone. Strained: a step of fatigue.
Agility Climb or jump: Climb a wall, jump a ditch, keep his feet on ice. Ordinary — Over. Not this way. Falls: roll a fall as a wound.
Endurance Endure: Keep going: swim, go without sleep, hold out in the cold. Ordinary — Holds out. A step of fatigue. Collapses, or goes under.
Wits Notice or remember: Recall a face, a road or a password; work something out. Ordinary — Yes. No. Remembers it wrong.
Nerve Keep his head: Stay calm out of a fight: under shelling in a dugout, at a hanging, before an officer. Ordinary — Steady. Shaken: −10 to his next check. Breaks: runs, freezes or lashes out.
Presence Impress: Stare a man down, make a first impression, be remembered. Ordinary the other man (Presence) He gives way. No effect. Made an enemy.

Wound tables

Each battle rolls its wounds on a table built from the record of that war, and these are the notes on where each one comes from. The tables themselves are in the printed tables and the wound roller. A gameplay-adjusted table is re-weighted from bone evidence to stand for every blow that landed, not only the ones that marked bone; an evidence table is the record itself.

Korea 1950-53 - hospitalized wounded

Location of wounds in US Army casualties admitted to hospital, Korean War.

How sure: taken directly from a source. Region totals are from the source. The split inside each region uses body exposure (design estimate).

Rolled by: the battlefields of Task Force Smith at Osan 1950, Fox Hill at Toktong Pass 1950, The perimeter at Chipyong-ni 1951, Hill 504 and the valley at Kapyong 1951, Hill 931 on Heartbreak Ridge 1951, Pork Chop Hill 1953; the armies of US 1950-51, US 1952-53, Commonwealth, ROK, Chinese, North Korea.

Battlefields

Each battlefield lays out on the field map under Battlefield. What follows is what the field and its phases hold, and, briefly, what happened there.

Task Force Smith at Osan, 5 July 1950

  • The armies: United Nations and North Koreans.
  • Fought for: the saddle where the road crosses the ridge, attacked by the North Koreans.
  • The field: 220 by 110 hexes of 10 m, about 2,200 by 950 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Overcast, calm or light air from the south.
  • Wounds: Korea 1950-53 - hospitalized wounded.
  • On the travel map: Osan, 1950 (Suwon to P'yongt'aek), at the saddle north of Osan (Jukmiryeong).

What happened

The North Korean tanks came down the road from Suwon at about eight in the morning and drove through the saddle under fire; a few were stopped, the rest went on south, cutting the telephone wire to the guns. Near noon the infantry followed, about 5,000 men, came on across the paddies under the mortars and howitzers, and worked round both flanks. At half past two Smith ordered the withdrawal; most of the losses came as the companies fell back across the open ground. About 150 of the infantry and 31 of the gunners were killed, wounded or missing. The North Koreans' losses are put at about 130.

How the field is drawn

Task Force Smith's position north of Osan, 5 July 1950, at 10 m a hex: 220 x 110 hexes, about 2200 m east to west and 950 m north to south, north at the top: the hill line across the middle, the highway over it at the saddle on the left, the railroad on the right, rice paddies before and behind. The hills, the saddle, the paddies and the line are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the infantry attack near noon, in our own words, with round numbers for play. A wet morning after rain; the paddies are deep in water. There are no vehicle rules: the T-34s are on call as tanks firing over open sights (Fire support), and the Americans' recoilless rifles and bazookas fight as riflemen. Their foxholes are men gone to ground: they start that way. Most of the force were young soldiers new to battle (green).

Fox Hill at Toktong Pass, 27-28 November 1950

  • The armies: United Nations and Chinese.
  • Fought for: the crest Fox Company held, attacked by the Chinese.
  • The field: 150 by 120 hexes of 10 m, about 1,500 by 1,040 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, strong wind from the north-west, night.
  • Wounds: Korea 1950-53 - hospitalized wounded.
  • On the travel map: Chosin Reservoir, 1950 (Yudam-ni to Hungnam), at Toktong Pass (Fox Hill).

What happened

Fox Company was posted on the hill on 27 November to hold the pass for the regiments at Yudam-ni. At 02:30 Chinese in about company strength struck the north, west and south of the perimeter and overran the 3rd Platoon's forward squads; fresh companies were fed in against the 2nd and 3rd Platoons, and Chinese walking down the road stumbled into the command post and the mortars. By 06:30 the attack was broken (Montross and Canzona). The Marines held the crest, lost and retook part of it, and held on for five days and nights, supplied by air drops and covered by the howitzers at Hagaru-ri and by Corsairs, until the 1st Battalion, 7th Marines reached them across the mountains on 2 December. Of about 240 men, 26 were killed, 89 wounded and 3 missing; many more suffered frostbite.

How the field is drawn

Fox Hill over Toktong Pass on the night of 27-28 November 1950, at 10 m a hex: 150 x 120 hexes, about 1500 m east to west and 1040 m north to south, north at the top: the hill Fox Company held in the middle, the road through the pass below it to the south, the heights to the north, a ridge across the road. The hill, road, rocks and slopes are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the first night's attack, in our own words, with round numbers for play. Bitter cold (-20 F): automatic weapons jam, men move slowly; deep snow; a dark night with a strong wind from the north-west. Corsairs fly only by day.

The perimeter at Chipyong-ni, 14-15 February 1951

  • The armies: United Nations and Chinese.
  • Fought for: G Company's hill on the southern perimeter, attacked by the Chinese.
  • The field: 200 by 170 hexes of 10 m, about 2,000 by 1,470 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, breeze from the north-west, night.
  • Wounds: Korea 1950-53 - hospitalized wounded.
  • On the travel map: Chipyong-ni, 1951 (Yangpyong to Wonju), at Chipyong-ni.

What happened

The Chinese came at the perimeter on the night of 13 February, from the north-west, north and south-east, and again all round after dark on the 14th, after a day in which fighter-bombers and an airdrop of ammunition kept them off. In the early hours of the 15th they broke into the southern perimeter at G Company's hill; counterattacks by the reserve, the Rangers and B Company could not retake all of it. That afternoon Task Force Crombez's tanks arrived from Yoju and the Chinese drew off. The 23rd lost about 50 killed, 250 wounded and 40 missing; the Chinese, by US estimates, some 2,000 killed.

How the field is drawn

The perimeter at Chipyong-ni on the night of 14-15 February 1951, at 10 m a hex: 200 x 170 hexes, about 2000 m east to west and 1470 m north to south, north at the top: the village in the middle, the railroad through its south, the road north and south, and the ring of low hills the 23rd Infantry dug in on, about a mile across. The hills, the village, the railroad and the paddies are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the second night's attack, in our own words, with round numbers for play. A clear, bitter night with snow on the ground and the paddies frozen hard (open ground). It is dark: fire the illumination (the transports' flares) or flares from the line to see what is coming. The fighter-bombers fly only by day.

Hill 504 and the valley at Kapyong, 23-24 April 1951

  • The armies: United Nations and Chinese.
  • Fought for: Hill 504's summit, attacked by the Chinese.
  • The field: 220 by 160 hexes of 10 m, about 2,200 by 1,390 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air, night.
  • Wounds: Korea 1950-53 - hospitalized wounded.
  • On the travel map: Kapyong, 1951 (the Kapyong valley), at Hill 504.
  • The record: the fight lasted about 871 exchanges (a minute each).

What happened

The ROK 6th Division broke on 22 April and streamed back down the valley. That night and the next the Chinese came after it. From 21:30 on the 23rd they struck the tanks' outpost and B Company in the valley and climbed the spurs at A and D Companies on the hill, attacking all night; the Australians held, and the next afternoon fell back through the Middlesex, the tanks covering them. 3 RAR lost 32 killed and 59 wounded; the Chinese far more.

How the field is drawn

Hill 504 and the Kapyong valley on the night of 23-24 April 1951, at 10 m a hex: 220 x 160 hexes, about 2200 m east to west and 1390 m north to south, north at the top: the valley with its paddies, road and river in the middle, B Company's knoll by the road, Hill 504's summit and spurs on the right, the hills towards 677 on the left, Chuktun-ni at the bottom. The hill, spurs, river, road and hamlet are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the night attack, in our own words, with round numbers for play. A dark night; the river is shallow and fordable (marsh).

Hill 931 on Heartbreak Ridge, October 1951

  • The armies: United Nations and North Koreans.
  • Fought for: Hill 931, attacked by the United Nations.
  • The field: 170 by 260 hexes of 10 m, about 1,700 by 2,250 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, breeze from the north-west.
  • Wounds: Korea 1950-53 - hospitalized wounded.
  • On the travel map: Heartbreak Ridge, 1951 (the Mundung-ni and Sat'ae-ri valleys), at Hill 931.
  • The record: the fight lasted about 901 exchanges (a minute each).

What happened

The 23rd Infantry and the French Battalion attacked up the ridge from 13 September 1951 and took and lost Hill 931 several times against North Koreans in bunkers, with heavy losses on both sides. In October the 2nd Division attacked along the whole front: the 23rd's 2nd Battalion went in along the crest on the night of 5 October with the 3rd behind it; by 03:00 they held the southern half of 931, and by day the French closed in from the north. Before noon Hill 931 was finally taken. From 10 October tanks went up the Mundung-ni valley behind the ridge, and the French took the last peak, Hill 851, at daybreak on 13 October. The tank company on this map came up the valley four days after 931 fell: the GM can leave it off.

How the field is drawn

Hill 931 on Heartbreak Ridge, October 1951, at 10 m a hex: 170 x 260 hexes, about 1700 m east to west and 2250 m north to south, north at the top: the narrow crest running north and south up the middle, Hill 931 in the upper part, Hill 894 at the bottom, spurs off both sides, the Mundung-ni valley along the west edge. The ridge, spurs, valley and bunkers are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the October attack, in our own words, with round numbers for play. Steep slopes of shattered trees and rock; the North Koreans' bunkers on the crest; tanks in the valley (vehicles). A fair autumn day.

Pork Chop Hill, 16-17 April 1953

  • The armies: United Nations and Chinese.
  • Fought for: the top of Pork Chop Hill, attacked by the Chinese.
  • The field: 160 by 130 hexes of 10 m, about 1,600 by 1,130 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air, night.
  • Wounds: Korea 1950-53 - hospitalized wounded.
  • On the travel map: Pork Chop Hill, 1953 (the outpost line north of Yeoncheon), at Pork Chop Hill.
  • The record: the fight lasted about 1496 exchanges (a minute each).

What happened

At about 23:00 on 16 April 1953 a Chinese battalion came up Pork Chop out of the dark and overran most of E Company's trenches. K Company counterattacked up the hill before dawn and L Company from Hill 200; companies of the 17th Infantry followed, and by the 18th the hill was back in American hands, after some 77,000 shells had been fired on the outposts. In April the Americans lost 104 killed and 373 wounded.

How the field is drawn

Pork Chop Hill on the night of 16-17 April 1953, at 10 m a hex: 160 x 130 hexes, about 1600 m east to west and 1130 m north to south, north at the top: Pork Chop in the middle, ringed with trenches and bunkers and wire, Hill 200 to the south-east, the main line's hills along the bottom, the valleys between cratered and wired. The hill, trenches, bunkers, valley and Hill 200 are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the Chinese attack, in our own words, with round numbers for play. A dark night: fire illumination and flares. The defenders wear the M1952 flak vest; the Chinese attack with burp guns (submachine guns) and grenades.

Landing zone X-Ray, 14 November 1965

  • The armies: United States and North Vietnamese.
  • Fought for: the landing zone, attacked by the North Vietnamese.
  • The field: 160 by 130 hexes of 10 m, about 1,600 by 1,130 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air.
  • Wounds: Vietnam 1965-70 - hospitalized wounded.
  • On the travel map: Ia Drang, 1965 (X-Ray and Albany), at Landing zone X-Ray.
  • The record: the fight lasted about 1346 exchanges (a minute each).

What happened

B Company landed at 10:48 and within the hour was fighting on the slopes west of the creek bed; its 2nd Platoon was cut off on a knoll and surrounded. A Company came in on its left, C Company to the south, and the North Vietnamese came down off the massif at all three. Artillery from Falcon, rocket helicopters and air strikes with napalm held them off while the rest of the battalion landed under fire; D Company came in during the afternoon and a company of the 2nd Battalion at dusk. The cut-off platoon held through the night and was reached the next afternoon. At X-Ray the Americans lost 79 killed and 121 wounded over three days; they counted 634 North Vietnamese dead.

How the field is drawn

Landing zone X-Ray on the afternoon of 14 November 1965, at 10 m a hex: 160 x 130 hexes, about 1600 m east to west and 1130 m north to south, north at the top: the clearing right of middle (the landing zone, H), the dry creek bed west of it, the lower slopes of the Chu Pong massif on the left, the knoll where B Company's 2nd Platoon was cut off up to the north-west. Light cover (scrub, key o): the tall elephant grass among the scrub trees (woods) round the clearing. The clearing, the creek bed, the knoll and the slopes are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is mid-afternoon of the 14th, as D Company was coming in, in our own words, with round numbers for play. Scrub trees, tall elephant grass and termite hills all round (woods, scrub, rough). D Company, and B Company of the 2nd Battalion at dusk, come in by air at the landing zone, 80 men an exchange, while the North Vietnamese are not on top of it; a hot landing zone costs men.

Hill 875, Dak To, 19 November 1967

  • The armies: United States and ARVN and North Vietnamese.
  • Fought for: the crest of Hill 875, attacked by the United States and ARVN.
  • The field: 120 by 140 hexes of 10 m, about 1,200 by 1,210 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air.
  • Wounds: Vietnam 1965-70 - hospitalized wounded.
  • On the travel map: Dak To, 1967 (the base to Hill 875), at Hill 875.
  • The record: the fight lasted about 5131 exchanges (a minute each).

What happened

On 19 November 1967 the 2nd Battalion, 503rd Infantry went up the north slope of Hill 875 and was stopped below the crest by the 174th Regiment's bunkers, while North Vietnamese came in behind it and overran the landing zone; that evening a stray bomb fell among the paratroopers. The 4th Battalion reached them the next night, and on 23 November, after days of air strikes, the two battalions took the crest.

How the field is drawn

Hill 875 near Dak To on 19 November 1967, at 10 m a hex: 120 x 140 hexes, about 1200 m east to west and 1210 m north to south, north at the top: the crest below the middle, ringed with bunkers and trenches, the north slope above it shattered bamboo and fallen trees, jungle all round. The hill, the slopes, the bunkers and the trenches are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the attack going up, in our own words, with round numbers for play. Fair and dry: the dry season had begun.

Hill 861A, Khe Sanh, 5 February 1968

  • The armies: United States and ARVN and North Vietnamese.
  • Fought for: the top of Hill 861A, attacked by the North Vietnamese.
  • The field: 140 by 120 hexes of 10 m, about 1,400 by 1,040 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fog, calm or light air, night.
  • Wounds: Vietnam 1965-70 - hospitalized wounded.
  • On the travel map: Khe Sanh, 1968 (the base and its hills), at Hill 861A.

What happened

At about 03:05 on 5 February 1968, as the base was shelled, about 200 North Vietnamese came through the wire on the north of Hill 861A and into E Company's trenches. At 05:00 Lieutenant Shanley's 1st Platoon, pushed out to its alternate positions, counterattacked and threw them out hand to hand; the survivors came again, half-heartedly, and were repulsed before dawn, with the base's guns firing round the hill; seven Marines were killed, and more than a hundred North Vietnamese dead were counted.

How the field is drawn

Hill 861A before dawn on 5 February 1968, at 10 m a hex: 140 x 120 hexes, about 1400 m east to west and 1040 m north to south, north at the top: the knoll in the middle, ringed with trenches, bunkers and wire, the ridge running down to the south-west towards Hill 861, the slopes cleared to elephant grass and craters, jungle beyond. Light cover (scrub, key o): the elephant grass on the cleared slopes, seen and shot through at a cost. The hill, the ridge, the trenches, bunkers and wire are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the North Vietnamese attack, in our own words, with round numbers for play. Fog and a dark night: fire illumination and flares.

Hue: the new city, 4-6 February 1968

  • The armies: United States and ARVN and North Vietnamese.
  • Fought for: the provincial headquarters, attacked by the United States and ARVN.
  • The field: 150 by 110 hexes of 10 m, about 1,500 by 950 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Rain, breeze from the north-east.
  • Wounds: Vietnam 1965-70 - hospitalized wounded.
  • On the travel map: Hue, 1968 (the city and Phu Bai), at Hue, the new city (south bank).
  • The record: the fight lasted about 3301 exchanges (a minute each).

What happened

From 4 February the 2nd Battalion, 5th Marines, with the 1st Battalion, 1st Marines, fought east from the MACV compound and the university, taking the Treasury, the public health building and the hospital building by building with tanks, Ontos, recoilless rifles and tear gas; the provincial headquarters fell on the 6th. By 10 February the south bank was clear, and the fighting moved into the Citadel.

How the field is drawn

The new city of Hue, south of the Perfume River, on 4-6 February 1968, at 10 m a hex: 150 x 110 hexes, about 1500 m east to west and 950 m north to south, north at the top: the river along the top with its bridge into the Citadel, Le Loi street and the park along the bank, Highway 1 coming up from the An Cuu bridge on the Phu Cam canal along the bottom, and between them blocks of houses and the stone public buildings: the MACV compound, the university, the provincial headquarters, the Treasury, the hospital and the prison. The streets, blocks and buildings are drawn by hand to that pattern, not traced from any map or photograph; the deployment is the Marines attacking east, in our own words, with round numbers for play. The public buildings are tall buildings (tall buildings) and the houses buildings, with rubble where the shells fell; tanks keep to the streets. Cold drizzle and low cloud.

Hamburger Hill (Dong Ap Bia), 20 May 1969

  • The armies: United States and ARVN and North Vietnamese.
  • Fought for: the summit of Hill 937 (Hamburger Hill), attacked by the United States and ARVN.
  • The field: 140 by 140 hexes of 10 m, about 1,400 by 1,210 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Overcast, calm or light air.
  • Wounds: Vietnam 1965-70 - hospitalized wounded.
  • On the travel map: Hamburger Hill, 1969 (the A Shau valley), at Dong Ap Bia (Hill 937).

What happened

On the morning of 20 May 1969, after ten days of attacks, the 3rd Battalion, 187th Infantry went up from the north-west, the 1st Battalion, 506th Infantry from the south and an ARVN battalion from the east. The North Vietnamese held their bunkers to the last or slipped away towards Laos, and the summit was taken about noon.

How the field is drawn

The summit of Dong Ap Bia (Hill 937) on 20 May 1969, at 10 m a hex: 140 x 140 hexes, about 1400 m east to west and 1210 m north to south, north at the top: the summit in the middle, stripped to stumps and craters, with tiers of bunkers down its slopes, the spurs running down to the north-west and the south, blasted jungle and bamboo below. The hill, its spurs and the bunkers are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the last assault, in our own words, with round numbers for play. Overcast, the slopes mud after days of rain.

A worked example: the squad

The Rules follow one medieval retinue. This chapter follows a US Army rifle squad in Vietnam through one night, with the same rules and the modules this book switches on and, where dice are rolled, the dice given. The team builder made the squad.

The squad

The team builder rolls a rifle squad. Ricky Garcia leads it: 3 terms, each a year of the war, so he is 21, with Command 90. Its machine gunner is Dennis Garcia, 2 terms, who fires the gun at 40% but defends at only 15%. Its grenadier is Daniel Miller, and its medic is John Washington, Leechcraft 41. 5 riflemen follow them. Their kit: M1 helmet, nylon flak vest (US Army M1952/M69, 1952-75).

On the field map

The squad: an ambush in the dark

The squad lies in extended order beside a trail on a dark night, gone to ground. No one can see to aim past 55 yards (50 m). Shots at the squad lose 15% for going to ground, and only 10% of the aimed ones find a man to aim at.

An enemy column comes down the trail. When the squad's gun opens fire, its muzzle flashes give it away: the enemy can now aim at its hex from up to 328 yards (300 m). The sergeant calls the company's mortars for illumination. It lands this exchange and lights the trail as by day for 2 exchanges, so his riflemen can aim.

In the roller

The heroes' wounds are rolled in full, as in the fight.

The squad: the gun

An enemy rifleman, a regular, fires his AK at Dennis at 50% and rolls 15: a margin of 35. Against a bullet, an arm takes a margin of 30 or more to be serious, so this one is serious. Dennis dodges at 15% and rolls 40: no.

The round strikes his upper arm (right), where his vest does not reach. It bleeds 2, pain 2, and the arm is hurt. The wound carries shock, so he makes a stop check: Nerve 60, less 2 steps of pain, gives 40. He rolls 22 and passes: he fights on.

But the machine gun takes both hands. With an arm hurt he cannot fire it, as in Wounds, so he can only defend. At 1 Blood a round, his 18 Blood lasts 18 rounds.

The squad: the grenade

A grenade bursts beside Daniel. The thrower's margin is 25 (he rolled 25). A fragment in the body is serious from a margin of 10, so this is serious, in his chest (left). But his vest, a nylon flak vest (M1952, M69), takes 2 steps off a fragment: it is stopped. Against a rifle round the same vest takes nothing.

The squad: the medic

In a quiet moment John crawls to the gun. He binds Dennis's arm at his Leechcraft 41 and rolls 12: he binds it, taking the bleeding down 2 steps to 0. The arm is still hurt (−20% to his attack with it), so another man takes the gun.

At dawn the squad carries him back. His wound goes onto the track as in Recovery.

For the GM

In a later war the heroes are the few men whose names the players know in a fight of hundreds. Keep the field map for the shape of the night and the roller for the moments that matter: a gunner hit, a medic crawling out, a vest that held.
